```{python}
import polars as pl
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect("lahmansbaseballdb.sqlite")
```

## Question 1: Top 10 Longest MLB Careers
Identify the top 10 players with the longest Major League Baseball careers. Include their:
      playerID,
      first_name,
      last_name,
      career_length.

```{python}
q1 = """
SELECT 
    b.playerID,
    MIN(b.yearID) AS first_year,
    MAX(b.yearID) AS last_year,
    MAX(b.yearID) - MIN(b.yearID) + 1 AS career_length
FROM Batting b
GROUP BY b.playerID
ORDER BY career_length DESC
LIMIT 10
"""
career_df = pl.read_database(q1, con)

people_df = pl.read_database("SELECT playerID, nameFirst, nameLast FROM People", con)

longest_careers = (
    career_df
    .join(people_df, on="playerID", how="left")
    .select([
        "playerID",
        pl.col("nameFirst").alias("first_name"),
        pl.col("nameLast").alias("last_name"),
        "career_length"
    ])
    .sort("career_length", descending=True)
)
longest_careers
```

## Question 2: Average Salary by Position

Write an SQL query that pulls the tables you need into a polars dataframe. Then, use python polars to create a summary table showing the average salary for each position (e.g., pitcher, catcher, outfielder). Position information can be found in the fielding table in the POS column.

Include the following columns:
     position,
     average_salary,
     total_players,
     highest_salary.

The highest_salary column should display the highest salary ever earned by a player in that position.
    Additionally, add a new column to the summary table you just created to label the average salary:
         If the average salary is above $3 million, categorize it as “High Salary.”
         If the average salary is between $2 million and $3 million, categorize it as “Medium Salary.” Otherwise, categorize it as “Low Salary.”
     Order the table by average salary in descending order.


```{python}
fielding_df = pl.read_database(
    "SELECT playerID, yearID, POS, CAST(G AS INTEGER) AS G FROM Fielding", con
)
salaries_df = pl.read_database(
    "SELECT playerID, yearID, CAST(salary AS REAL) AS salary FROM Salaries", con
)

primary_pos = (
    fielding_df
    .group_by(["playerID", "yearID", "POS"])
    .agg(pl.col("G").sum().alias("games"))
    .sort("games", descending=True)
    .unique(subset=["playerID", "yearID"], keep="first")
    .select(["playerID", "yearID", "POS"])
)

salary_pos = (
    salaries_df
    .join(primary_pos, on=["playerID", "yearID"], how="inner")
    .select(["playerID", "yearID", "salary", "POS"])
)

pos_summary = (
    salary_pos
    .group_by("POS")
    .agg([
        pl.col("salary").mean().alias("average_salary"),
        pl.col("playerID").n_unique().alias("total_players"),
        pl.col("salary").max().alias("highest_salary")
    ])
    .filter(pl.col("POS").is_not_null())
    .sort("average_salary", descending=True)
)

pos_summary = pos_summary.with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("average_salary") > 3_000_000)
      .then(pl.lit("High Salary"))
      .when(pl.col("average_salary").is_between(2_000_000, 3_000_000))
      .then(pl.lit("Medium Salary"))
      .otherwise(pl.lit("Low Salary"))
      .alias("salary_category")
)

pos_summary = pos_summary.rename({"POS": "position"})
pos_summary.select([
    "position",
    pl.col("average_salary").round(0).alias("avg_salary"),
    "total_players",
    "highest_salary",
    "salary_category"
])
```

Summary of my findings: 
The top ten longest careers in MLB last well over decades, with some even exceeding 30 years. This means that the players had made their debuts when they were relatively young or still played well into their forties. In terms of salary analysis, pitchers, catchers, and outfielders make up the high-salary groups. Infielders, which include first base, second base, third base, and shortstop, as well as designated hitters are categorized under medium or low salaries. By forcing the position classification of the salary per player-year to just one based on the most games played per year, this ensured that there was no double counting for utility players. Naturally, the highest salaries would be earned by superstar pitchers or outfielders.
